quick: 1-2 drops in the eye(s) up to 4 times daily (0.05%)
Use only if clearly needed; minimal systemic exposure topically
summary: Tetrahydrozoline is an imidazoline alpha-adrenergic agonist used as a topical vasoconstrictor, most commonly as ophthalmic drops (e.g. Visine) to relieve redness of the eye due to minor irritation. It works by constricting superficial conjunctival blood vessels. It is intended for short-term, occasional use; overuse causes rebound redness (conjunctival hyperaemia). Ingestion - especially in children - can cause serious systemic alpha-adrenergic toxicity (CNS depression, bradycardia, hypotension), so it must be kept out of reach.
indications: Temporary relief of redness of the eye due to minor eye irritation (ophthalmic)
Temporary relief of nasal congestion (nasal formulations, where marketed)

dosage.c: Ophthalmic redness relief (adults and children >=6 years)
dosage.d: 1-2 drops of 0.05% solution in the affected eye(s) up to 4 times daily
dosage.n: Short-term use only; do not exceed labelled frequency

dosage.d: Use for no more than about 72 hours of regular use
Not recommended without physician direction; risk of systemic toxicity if ingested
dosage.n: Keep out of reach of children

admin: Wash hands; tilt the head back and instill into the conjunctival sac without touching the eye
Use only for short-term relief of minor redness, not for prolonged or daily use
Remove contact lenses before instillation and follow product guidance on reinsertion
Do not use if the solution changes colour or becomes cloudy
Keep tightly closed and out of reach of children - ingestion is dangerous
moa: Tetrahydrozoline is a sympathomimetic imidazoline that stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors on the smooth muscle of blood vessels. Local application produces vasoconstriction of the dilated conjunctival (or nasal mucosal) vessels, reducing redness and congestion. It has little effect on the underlying pupil at usual ophthalmic doses.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to tetrahydrozoline or other imidazolines
Narrow-angle (closed-angle) glaucoma or anatomically narrow angles (ophthalmic)
relative: Concurrent or recent (within 14 days) MAO inhibitor use
monitor: Eye pain, vision changes or persistent redness

preg: Systemic exposure from correct ophthalmic use is minimal; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Avoid prolonged or excessive use.
lact: Limited data; systemic absorption from topical ocular use is low. Use with caution while breastfeeding.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for topical use; systemic exposure is minimal.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed for topical use; systemic exposure is minimal.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - risk of hypertensive crisis if significant systemic absorption occurs; avoid concurrent use
moderate: Other sympathomimetics or beta-blockers - additive or opposing cardiovascular effects if absorbed
Tricyclic antidepressants - potentiation of pressor effects
interactions.alcohol: No clinically relevant interaction with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: No relevant effect on laboratory tests at topical doses.

serious: Rebound conjunctival hyperaemia (worsening redness) with prolonged use
Precipitation of acute angle-closure glaucoma in predisposed eyes
Systemic sympathomimetic effects (palpitations, hypertension) with excessive absorption
emergency: Accidental ingestion (especially in children): CNS depression, lethargy, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia - seek emergency care

monitoring: Symptom relief and avoidance of overuse/rebound
Persistent or worsening redness, eye pain or vision change (warrants evaluation)
Systemic signs if accidental ingestion is suspected
counsel: Use only for short-term relief of minor eye redness, no more than a few days
Using it too often makes the redness worse (rebound) - stop and see a clinician if redness persists
Do not use if you have glaucoma or eye pain without checking with a clinician
Keep well out of reach of children - swallowing even a small amount can be dangerous
pk: Vasoconstriction (redness relief) within minutes of instillation
Topical pharmacokinetics not well characterised; systemic levels normally negligible
Store at room temperature; keep the bottle tightly closed and away from children
pearls: Topical ophthalmic decongestant for minor eye redness - short-term, occasional use only
Overuse causes rebound conjunctival hyperaemia (a 'rebound redness' cycle)
Ingestion is a recognised paediatric poisoning hazard - small volumes cause CNS depression, bradycardia and hypotension; store safely
Avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and with MAO inhibitors
Persistent redness, pain or vision change needs proper ophthalmic assessment, not continued drops
missed: Used as needed for symptom relief, so there is no fixed dosing schedule to miss; simply use a dose when symptoms occur, without exceeding the labelled frequency or duration.
overdose: Topical overdose may cause stinging and rebound redness. Ingestion (notably in children) can cause serious systemic toxicity - drowsiness, coma, bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia; this is a medical emergency requiring supportive care and observation. Contact a poison control centre and seek emergency treatment.
